pos: adv. (obscurely, dimly, as in a riddle)
etymology: From dark, Old English deorc, plus -ly. In 1 Corinthians 13:12 it renders the Greek en ainigmati, in a riddle, in an enigma.
biblical_def: Paul's great chapter on charity closes with a contrast between knowledge now and knowledge then. “For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known” (1 Corinthians 13:12). The glass is a mirror of polished metal, which gave a true but dim image; the word rendered darkly means in a riddle. Present knowledge of God is real, but partial and indirect. Paul had already said why it is temporary: “But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Corinthians 13:10). Yet the dimness is not darkness. The same apostle says believers even now, “with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18). We see darkly, but we see; and what we see changes us.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): D'ARKLY, adverb Obscurely; dimly; blindly; uncertainly; with imperfect light, clearness or knowledge.
webster_full: D'ARKLY, adverb Obscurely; dimly; blindly; uncertainly; with imperfect light, clearness or knowledge.
They learn only what tradition has darkly conveyed to them. Anon.
In 1 Corinthians 13:12 it renders the Greek en ainigmati, in a riddle.
Paul sets seeing darkly against seeing face to face.
The glass is a mirror of polished metal.
scriptures: For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away.
But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.
corruption_summary: Darkly is made the motto of a fashionable agnosticism that says nothing certain can be known about God, when Paul's point is that true knowledge, though partial, is given now and will be perfected.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary religious writing loves to quote through a glass, darkly as a warrant for permanent uncertainty: since no one sees clearly, no doctrine can be held firmly, and humility means holding every belief loosely. That is not Paul's argument. He knows in part, but what he knows he knows truly, and he wrote thirteen letters of doctrine with apostolic authority.

The principle to recover is the clarity and sufficiency of Scripture. God has revealed Himself truly in His word, though not exhaustively; the believer's knowledge is partial but not false, and it waits for the face-to-face sight of the beatific vision.

roots_lines: Old English deorc, dark, obscure.

partial knowledge, but true

etymology: Latin demonstratio, from demonstrare, to point out, show, from de- and monstrare, to show. Greek apodeixis, a showing forth, a proof.
biblical_def: Paul reminds the Corinthians how he first came to them. He did not arrive with polished oratory: “And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1 Corinthians 2:4). The proof of his message was not rhetorical skill but the Spirit's work in convicting and converting sinners through the plain preaching of Christ crucified. He gives the reason: “That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:5). He wrote the same of Thessalonica: “For our gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Ghost, and in much assurance” (1 Thessalonians 1:5). The Spirit's demonstration is the gospel proving itself in changed lives, and it is the only kind of proof on which saving faith can safely stand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DEMONSTRATION, noun 1. The act of demonstrating, or of exhibiting certain proof.
webster_full: DEMONSTRATION, noun 1. The act of demonstrating, or of exhibiting certain proof.

2. The highest degree of evidence; certain proof exhibited, or such proof as establishes a fact or proposition beyond a possibility of doubt, or as shows the contrary position to be absurd or impossible.

3. Indubitable evidence of the senses, or of reason; evidence which satisfies the mind of the certainty of a fact or proposition. Thus we hold that the works of nature exhibit demonstration of the existence of a God.
4. In logic, a series of syllogisms, all whose premises are either definitions, self-evident truths, or propositions already established.
5. Show; exhibition.
scriptures: And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.
For our gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Ghost, and in much assurance; as ye know what manner of men we were among you for your sake.
corruption_summary: Demonstration of the Spirit and of power is claimed for staged signs and wonders, when Paul meant the Spirit's converting power working through the preaching of Christ crucified.
corruption_paragraphs: Signs-and-wonders movements, from the Third Wave of the 1980s to contemporary power-evangelism ministries, cite 1 Corinthians 2:4 to argue that preaching must be accompanied by visible miracles to be authentic. Paul's contrast is not between preaching and miracles but between man's wisdom and God's power, and the power he names is the power of the cross to save (1 Corinthians 1:18).

The dictionary is cessationist. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of the preached word: faith comes by hearing, and the Spirit demonstrates His power when sinners are made new creatures under the gospel.
roots_summary: Latin demonstratio, a pointing out; Greek apodeixis, a showing forth.
roots_lines: Latin de-, out, and monstrare, to show.
Greek apodeixis, proof by display, used once in the New Testament.

1 Corinthians 2:5 grounds faith in the power of God.

not with enticing words of man's wisdom

etymology: Latin experimentum, from experiri, to try, test. In 2 Corinthians 9:13 it renders the Greek dokime, proof, tested character.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses experiment once, in its older sense of proof by trial. Paul was gathering the collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem, and he saw in it more than relief: “For the administration of this service not only supplieth the want of the saints, but is abundant also by many thanksgivings unto God” (2 Corinthians 9:12). The giving itself would be a test that proved the reality of the Corinthians' faith: “Whiles by the experiment of this ministration they glorify God for your professed subjection unto the gospel of Christ, and for your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men” (2 Corinthians 9:13). The Jewish believers would see Gentile money and know that Gentile faith was real. Paul had said the same earlier: he spoke “to prove the sincerity of your love” (2 Corinthians 8:8). Generosity is the experiment that shows whether a profession of the gospel is genuine.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): EXPER'IMENT, noun [Latin experimentum, from experior, as in experience, which see.] A trial; an act or operation designed to discover some unknown truth, principle or effect, or to establish it when discovered.
webster_full: EXPER'IMENT, noun [Latin experimentum, from experior, as in experience, which see.] A trial; an act or operation designed to discover some unknown truth, principle or effect, or to establish it when discovered. Experiments in chimistry disclose the qualities of natural bodies.

EXPER'IMENT, verb intransitive To make trial; to make an experiment; to operate on a body in such a manner as to discover some unknown fact, or to establish it when known. Philosophers experiment on natural bodies for the discovery of their qualities and combinations.
1. To try; to search by trial.
2. To experience. [Not used.]
EXPER'IMENT, verb transitive To try; to know by trial. [Not used.]
scriptures: Whiles by the experiment of this ministration they glorify God for your professed subjection unto the gospel of Christ, and for your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men;
For the administration of this service not only supplieth the want of the saints, but is abundant also by many thanksgivings unto God;
I speak not by commandment, but by occasion of the forwardness of others, and to prove the sincerity of your love.
corruption_summary: Experiment is turned into a spiritual method, faith as a trial run on God, when Scripture's experiment is the proving of a professed faith by its fruit.
corruption_paragraphs: Some popular teaching invites people to try Christianity as an experiment, or to test God with a pledge to see whether He will pay them back, a theme of prosperity preaching. Paul's experiment is the reverse. The giver is not testing God; God is proving the giver, and the result is thanksgiving to God, not profit to man.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a true profession of faith is evidenced by works. Love that gives liberally is the proof of subjection to the gospel of Christ.

roots_lines: Latin experiri, to try, test.

etymology: Latin intelligentia, from intelligere, to understand, from inter, between, and legere, to choose, gather. In Daniel 11:30 it renders the Hebrew bin, to discern, give heed to.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses intelligence once, in Webster's sense of secret communication between parties. Daniel's vision traces the career of a king of the north, fulfilled in Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who returned from a frustrated campaign in Egypt to vent his rage on Jerusalem. “For the ships of Chittim shall come against him: therefore he shall be grieved, and return, and have indignation against the holy covenant: so shall he do; he shall even return, and have intelligence with them that forsake the holy covenant” (Daniel 11:30). He would court the apostates within Israel and use them against the faithful: “And such as do wickedly against the covenant shall he corrupt by flatteries: but the people that do know their God shall be strong, and do exploits” (Daniel 11:32). The enemy outside always looks for allies inside. The defence is the knowledge of God, which makes the faithful strong, for “the wise shall understand” (Daniel 12:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): INTEL'LIGENCE, noun [Latin intelligentia, from intelligo, to understand. This verb is probably composed of in, inter, or intus, within, and lego to collect.
webster_full: INTEL'LIGENCE, noun [Latin intelligentia, from intelligo, to understand. This verb is probably composed of in, inter, or intus, within, and lego to collect. The primary sense of understand is generally to take or hold, as we say, to take one's ideas or meaning.]
1. Understanding; skill.
2. Notice; information communicated; an account of things distant or before unknown. intelligence may be transmitted by messengers, by letters, by signals or by telegraphs.

3. Commerce of acquaintance; terms of intercourse. Good intelligence between men is harmony. So we say, there is a good understanding between persons, when they have the same views, or are free from discord.
4. A spiritual being; as a created intelligence It is believed that the universe is peopled with innumerable superior intelligences.
scriptures: For the ships of Chittim shall come against him: therefore he shall be grieved, and return, and have indignation against the holy covenant: so shall he do; he shall even return, and have intelligence with them that forsake the holy covenant.
And such as do wickedly against the covenant shall he corrupt by flatteries: but the people that do know their God shall be strong, and do exploits.
Many shall be purified, and made white, and tried; but the wicked shall do wickedly: and none of the wicked shall understand; but the wise shall understand.
corruption_summary: Daniel 11 is dated after the events it describes because its accuracy is thought impossible for prophecy, when its precision is exactly what predictive prophecy looks like.
corruption_paragraphs: Because Daniel 11 traces the wars of the Ptolemies and Seleucids in such detail, critical scholarship assigns the book to an anonymous writer under Antiochus Epiphanes around 165 BC, who wrote history disguised as prophecy. The dictionary holds one Daniel of the sixth century BC, writing true prediction by revelation, as Christ Himself affirmed when He spoke of Daniel the prophet (Matthew 24:15).

The principle to recover is vigilance against collusion. Antiochus did his worst through those within the covenant people who forsook it; the church is most endangered when its own members have intelligence with its enemies.

etymology: Latin determinatio, a boundary, a conclusion, from determinare, to set bounds, from de- and terminus, a limit. In Zephaniah 3:8 it renders the Hebrew mishpat, judgment, decision.
biblical_def: Zephaniah's book moves from the day of wrath to the day of joy, and the hinge is God's determination. “Therefore wait ye upon me, saith the LORD, until the day that I rise up to the prey: for my determination is to gather the nations, that I may assemble the kingdoms, to pour upon them mine indignation, even all my fierce anger” (Zephaniah 3:8). God's purpose is fixed; His decree is His judgment. Yet the next verse shows what lies on the other side of the fire: “For then will I turn to the people a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the LORD, to serve him with one consent” (Zephaniah 3:9). Judgment and salvation flow from one settled purpose. The supreme instance is the cross, where Peter says Christ was “delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23). God's determination does not wait on man's decisions; man's worst decision served it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DETERMINATION, noun 1. The act of determining or deciding.
webster_full: DETERMINATION, noun 1. The act of determining or deciding.
2. Decision of a question in the mind; firm resolution; settled purpose; as, they have acquainted me with their determination
3. Judicial decision; the ending of a controversy or suit by the judgment of a court. Justice is promoted by a speedy determination of causes, civil and criminal.
4. Absolute direction to a certain end. Remissness can by no means consist with a constant determination of the will to the greatest apparent good.
5. An ending; a putting an end to; as the determination of a will.
scriptures: Zep 3:8

Therefore wait ye upon me, saith the LORD, until the day that I rise up to the prey: for my determination is to gather the nations, that I may assemble the kingdoms, to pour upon them mine indignation, even all my fierce anger: for all the earth shall be devoured with the fire of my jealousy.
Zep 3:9
For then will I turn to the people a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the LORD, to serve him with one consent.
Act 2:23
Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain:
corruption_summary: Open theism makes God's purposes provisional, revisable as the future unfolds, when Scripture speaks of His determination and determinate counsel as fixed.
corruption_paragraphs: Open theists such as Clark Pinnock, Gregory Boyd and John Sanders teach that the future is partly unknown even to God, and that His plans adjust to free human choices. Acts 2:23 alone refutes them: the most wicked free act in history, the crucifixion, was delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and the guilt of the wicked hands was not lessened by it.

The principle to recover is the eternal decree. The 1689 Confession, chapter 3, says God hath decreed in Himself from all eternity whatsoever comes to pass, yet so as thereby is God neither the author of sin nor is violence offered to the will of the creature.

etymology: Latin descriptio, from describere, to write down, copy, mark out, from de- and scribere, to write. In Joshua 18:6 it renders the Hebrew kathab, to write, a written survey.
biblical_def: After the conquest, seven tribes had not yet received their inheritance, and Joshua rebuked their slackness. He sent three men from each tribe to survey the land: “Ye shall therefore describe the land into seven parts, and bring the description hither to me, that I may cast lots for you here before the LORD our God” (Joshua 18:6). The description was a written survey of the remaining territory, city by city. The men did it: “And the men went and passed through the land, and described it by cities into seven parts in a book, and came again to Joshua to the host at Shiloh” (Joshua 18:9). Then the lot was cast before the LORD at Shiloh. Human diligence and divine disposal worked together: men wrote the description, and God gave the inheritance by lot. David later sang of the result in every believer's life: “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage” (Psalm 16:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DESCRIPTION, noun 1. The act of delineating, or representing the figure of any thing by a plan, to be presented to the eye.
webster_full: DESCRIPTION, noun 1. The act of delineating, or representing the figure of any thing by a plan, to be presented to the eye.
2. The figure or appearance of any thing delineated, or represented by visible lines, marks, colors, etc.; as the description of a country, or of Solomons temple.

3. The act of representing a thing by words or by signs, or the passage containing such representation; a representation of names, nature of properties, that gives to another a view of the thing. Homer abounds with beautiful and striking descriptions.
4. A definition. All definitions must be less perfect descriptions of a material thing, than a visible figure or delineation.
5. The qualities expressed in a representation; as, a man of this description Hence,

Psa 16:6

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. Joshua 18 is sometimes treated as late administrative fiction, but its procedure of survey, record and lot is exactly what the conquest narrative requires and what the boundary lists in the following chapters preserve.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is diligence in receiving what God gives. Seven tribes delayed to possess their inheritance; the cure was work and then submission to the lot that the LORD disposes.

pos: v.t. (to make able; to give power or ability)
etymology: From en-, to make, and able, from Latin habilis, fit, handy. In 1 Timothy 1:12 it renders the Greek endunamoo, to strengthen, to put power into.
biblical_def: Paul thanks Christ for his ministry and gives the whole credit away. “And I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who hath enabled me, for that he counted me faithful, putting me into the ministry” (1 Timothy 1:12). The order matters: Christ enabled, Christ counted, Christ put him in. The man He enabled had nothing to bring: “Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Timothy 1:13). The Greek word is the same Paul uses in Philippians 4:13, I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me. Ministry is not human talent improved by grace but grace creating a capacity that did not exist. Paul says it again to Corinth: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God” (2 Corinthians 3:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ENABLE, verb transitive [Norm. enhabler; en and hable, able. See Able.]
webster_full: ENABLE, verb transitive [Norm. enhabler; en and hable, able. See Able.]

1. To make able; to supply with power, physical or moral; to furnish with sufficient power or ability. By strength a man is enabled to work. Learning and industry enable men to investigate the laws of nature. Fortitude enables us to bear pain without murmuring.
2. To supply with means. Wealth enables men to be charitable, or to live in luxury.
3. To furnish with legal ability or competency; to authorize. The law enables us to dispose of our property by will.
4. To furnish with competent knowledge or skill, and in general, with adequate means.
scriptures: And I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who hath enabled me, for that he counted me faithful, putting me into the ministry;
Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God;
corruption_summary: Enabling grace is made the help God offers a will that must then decide for itself, when Paul's Christ enables, counts and puts into service by His own initiative.
corruption_paragraphs: Arminian theology speaks of prevenient grace that enables every man to believe, leaving the decisive act with the human will. Paul's account of his own conversion and calling allows no such division: the blasphemer and persecutor obtained mercy, and Christ enabled him. Grace in Scripture does not merely make salvation possible; it makes the sinner willing in the day of God's power.

The word enabler has also acquired a modern therapeutic sense, one who shields another from the consequences of sin; that is a distinct entry. The principle to recover here is monergism: our sufficiency is of God.

pos: v.t. (to meet in opposition; to engage in dispute)
etymology: Old French encontrer, from Latin in- and contra, against. In Acts 17:18 it renders the Greek sumballo, to throw together, to confer, dispute with.
biblical_def: In Athens Paul disputed in the synagogue and daily in the market, and the city's philosophers took him on. “Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection” (Acts 17:18). The Epicureans held that the gods were distant and death was the end; the Stoics held a divine reason pervading all things. Paul met both with the Creator, the coming judgment and the risen Man. The reaction was divided: “And when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter” (Acts 17:32). Paul's encounter is the pattern Peter commends: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear” (1 Peter 3:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ENCOUNT'ER, noun [Latin contra, against, or rather rencontre.]
webster_full: ENCOUNT'ER, noun [Latin contra, against, or rather rencontre.]
1. A meeting, particularly a sudden or accidental meeting of two or more persons. To shun th' encounter of the vulgar crowd.
2. A meeting in contest; a single combat, on a sudden meeting of parties; sometimes less properly, a duel.

3. A fight; a conflict; a skirmish; a battle; but more generally, a fight between a small number of men, or an accidental meeting and fighting of detachments, rather than a set battle or general engagement.
4. Eager and warm conversation, either in love or anger.
scriptures: Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection.
And when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
corruption_summary: Encounter has become the vocabulary of experiential religion, meeting God in feeling and atmosphere, when Paul's encounter at Athens was a reasoned contest of truth claims.
corruption_paragraphs: Charismatic and revivalist circles speak constantly of encounters with God, by which they mean intense subjective experiences sought in music, ministry times and prayer rooms. The word in Scripture describes something else: philosophers engaging an apostle in argument over the resurrection of Jesus.

The principle to recover is the reasonableness of the faith. The gospel meets unbelief with proclamation and reasons, grounded in the fact of the resurrection; and God meets His people by His word and Spirit in the ordinary means of grace, not in manufactured experiences.

etymology: From order, Latin ordo, a row, rank, plus -ly. In Acts 21:24 it renders the Greek stoicheo, to walk in line, to keep step.
biblical_def: When Paul reached Jerusalem for the last time, the elders told him that thousands of Jewish believers had heard that he taught Jews to forsake Moses. They proposed a public answer: Paul should join four men under a vow and pay their charges. “Them take, and purify thyself with them, and be at charges with them, that they may shave their heads: and all may know that those things, whereof they were informed concerning thee, are nothing; but that thou thyself also walkest orderly, and keepest the law” (Acts 21:24). To walk orderly is to keep in line, to walk by rule. Paul's letters use the same image for the Christian life, and its opposite: “withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us” (2 Thessalonians 3:6). And of the church's worship: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40). God is not the author of confusion, and His people walk in step with His word.
webster_full: OR'DERLY, adjective 1. Methodical; regular
2. Observant of order or method.
3. Well regulated; performed in good order; not tumultuous; as an orderly march.
4. According to established method.

5. Not unruly; not inclined to break from inclosures; peaceable. We say, cattle are orderly Orderly book, in military affairs, a book for every company, in which the sergeants write general and regimental orders. Orderly sergeant, a military officer who attends on a superior officer.
scriptures: Them take, and purify thyself with them, and be at charges with them, that they may shave their heads: and all may know that those things, whereof they were informed concerning thee, are nothing; but that thou thyself also walkest orderly, and keepest the law.
Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Decently and in order is quoted to justify any custom a church finds tidy, when Paul's order is the order God commands in His word.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 14:40 has been used to defend elaborate liturgies, vestments and church calendars on the ground that they are orderly. Paul's order was not aesthetic but regulative: in context he silences tongues without interpretation and governs prophets, and he says the things he writes are the commandments of the Lord (1 Corinthians 14:37).

The principle to recover is the regulative principle of worship and the ordered walk of the believer. What God commands is done in order; what He has not commanded is not added, however orderly it looks.

pos: n. pl. (written works; especially the books of Scripture)
etymology: From write, Old English writan, to score, inscribe, plus -ing. In John 5:47 it renders the Greek grammata, letters, writings.
biblical_def: Jesus closed a long debate with the Jewish leaders by summoning Moses as His witness. “For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me” (John 5:46). Then the sharpest question: “But if ye believe not his writings, how shall ye believe my words?” (John 5:47). The Lord treats the books of Moses as Moses' own writings, as true, and as testimony to Himself. He did the same after the resurrection on the road to Emmaus: “And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). The writings of the Old Testament and the words of Christ stand or fall together. A man cannot reject Moses and keep Jesus, because Jesus Himself vouched for Moses.

WRITING, noun 1. The act or art of forming letters and characters, on paper, wood, stone or other material, for the purpose of recording the ideas which characters and the words express, or of communicating them to others by visible signs.
2. Any thing written or expressed in letters; hence, any legal instrument, as a deed, a receipt, a bond, an agreement, etc.
3. A book; any written composition; a pamphlet; as the writings of Addison.

corruption_summary: Critical scholarship dissolves the writings of Moses into anonymous sources compiled centuries later, when Christ Himself said Moses wrote of Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Since the nineteenth century the dominant critical school has denied that Moses wrote the Pentateuch, assigning it to several hypothetical source documents edited after the exile. Christ's words in John 5:46-47 settle the question for those who receive Him: He calls them Moses' writings and says Moses wrote of Him.
The principle to recover is Mosaic authorship and the unity of Christ's authority with the Scriptures. To believe Christ is to believe the writings He believed.
